rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midpoint temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to test which crowded pairs respond to slope. This should spread the central cluster and reveal whether temperature changes will also be needed.
Keep the shallower gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity at the remaining unresolved pair. Higher temperature should also bring the last peak closer to the 10-minute target.

Test an intermediate temperature to separate the pair coincident at 60 C while retaining the selectivity gained over 40 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect before trimming retention time.

At 60 C, test a moderately steeper gradient to move the co-eluting pair apart through its differing slope responses. This also shortens the run while checking whether the central pair retains adequate resolution.

Shorten the gradient another two minutes to increase separation of the remaining critical pair, which improved markedly from 24 to 20 minutes. Monitor the central pairs, whose resolution is approaching the 1.5 threshold as the gradient steepens.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to slightly flatten the gradient and adjust selectivity around the nearly resolved central pair. This should preserve ample time margin while testing whether all pairs can clear 1.5 together.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 to lift both central pairs toward full resolution while preserving the late pair's margin. The lower endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window, so all eight peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the marginal central pairs above 1.5 while retaining the late pair's resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the last peak's estimated elution fraction, with elution expected well before 10 minutes.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the reference method. Test a higher starting fraction with a narrower gradient window to shorten elution, using the shallower slope to help preserve central-pair resolution while checking the late critical pair.

Keep injection 9 as the maximum-score reference and test the unexplored low-temperature selectivity with its gradient unchanged. This probes whether a different elution-order pattern offers wider resolution margins for subsequent acceleration.

Raise temperature one step from injection 11 to shift the remaining close pair and shorten retention. This tests a second potentially fully resolved region while preserving injection 9 as the maximum-score fallback.

Return to the high-temperature region and slightly flatten injection 10's slope to improve its unresolved central pair. The narrower window should keep the last peak within the gradient while testing a faster alternative to the maximum-score reference.

Test intermediate-temperature selectivity with the trimmed gradient, since changing the starting fraction can move the crossings seen in the earlier 40 C run. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score reference; this probes another resolution region that may permit further acceleration.

Test a substantially steeper gradient in the low-temperature selectivity region to seek a faster, reordered separation rather than making further marginal changes near 60 C. Injection 9 remains the established maximum-score method.

Test a steeper gradient to increase separation after the central pair's apparent order reversal, with a modest temperature increase to improve the late pair. This explores a faster separation while retaining injection 9 as the proven maximum-score method.

Lower temperature one step with the fast gradient unchanged to test whether the crowded central cluster opens through temperature-dependent selectivity. Monitor the late pair, which may lose resolution on cooling; injection 9 remains the maximum-score reference.

Test a higher starting fraction with a substantially shallower gradient to seek a different selectivity balance and shorter fully resolved separation. Injection 9 already attains the maximum CRF and remains the reference if this narrower window compromises resolution.

Shift injection 15's solvent window upward while preserving its gradient slope to test starting-composition selectivity in the low-temperature region. This may separate its central critical pair and shorten retention; injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score method.

Raise the starting fraction further at the same slope to continue opening the central pair, and increase temperature one step to improve the late pair. Check whether the neighboring central separation remains adequate as retention shortens; injection 9 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Cool one step to open injection 20's remaining central pair, while reducing the slope to support the late pair that loses resolution on cooling. This tests whether the fast, high-starting-fraction region can match injection 9's maximum score.

Raise the starting fraction to shorten the fully resolved separation from injection 21, while flattening the slope to protect the marginal late pair. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, and injection 21 is the fastest proven maximum-score reference.

Increase the gradient slope from 0.050 to 0.055 organic fraction per minute to shorten elution from injection 22, testing its central and late resolution margins. Injection 22 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method if either pair falls below 1.5.

Test a higher starting fraction for faster elution, paired with a substantially shallower slope to compensate for compression of the critical central pair. Injection 22 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method if this tradeoff fails.

Preserve injection 22's successful starting fraction, temperature, and slope while trimming the unused gradient tail. The gradient reaches its endpoint at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the expected last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this shorter program should retain the maximum CRF.
